text: Officer: This is the man; do thy office.
Officer: Antonio, I arrest thee at the suit
Of Count Orsino.
Antonio: You do mistake me, sir.
1 Officer: No, sir, no jot; I know your favour well, 5
Though now you have no sea-cap on your head.
Take him away; he knows I know him well.
Antonio: I must obey. [To VIOLA] This comes with seeking you;
But there’s no remedy; I shall answer it.
What will you do, now my necessity 10
Makes me to ask you for my purse? It grieves me
Much more for what I cannot do for you
Than what befalls myself. You stand amaz’d;
But be of comfort.
2 Officer: Come, sir, away. 15
Antonio: I must entreat of you some of that money.
Viola: What money, sir?
For the fair kindness you have show’d me here,
And part being prompted by your present trouble,
Out of my lean and low ability 20
I’ll lend you something. My having is not much;
I’ll make division of my present with you;
Hold, there’s half my coffer.
Antonio: Will you deny me now?
Is’t possible that my deserts to you 25
Can lack persuasion? Do not tempt my misery,
Lest that it make me so unsound a man
As to upbraid you with those kindnesses
That I have done for you.
Viola: I know of none, 30
Nor know I you by voice or any feature.
I hate ingratitude more in a man
Than lying, vainness, babbling drunkenness,
Or any taint of vice whose strong corruption
Inhabits our frail blood. 35
Antonio: O heavens themselves!
2 Officer: Come, sir, I pray you go.
Antonio: Let me speak a little. This youth that you see here
I snatch’d one half out of the jaws of death,
Reliev’d him with such sanctity of love, 40
And to his image, which methought did promise
Most venerable worth, did I devotion.
1 Officer: What’s that to us? The time goes by; away.
Antonio: But, O, how vile an idol proves this god!
Thou hast, Sebastian, done good feature shame. 45
In nature there’s no blemish but the mind:
None can be call’d deform’d but the unkind.
Virtue is beauty; but the beauteous evil
Are empty trunks, o’erflourish’d by the devil.
1 Officer: The man grows mad. Away with him. 50
Come, come, sir.
Antonio: Lead me on.
[Exit with OFFICERS.]
Viola: Methinks his words do from such passion fly
That he believes himself; so do not I. 55
Prove true, imagination, O, prove true,
That I, dear brother, be now ta’en for you!
(from Act 3, Scene 4)
How does Shakespeare make this moment in the play so dramatic?
Or 4(b) In what ways does Shakespeare movingly portray Viola’s love for Orsino?
WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE: Othello
Remember to support your ideas with details from the writing.
Either 5(a) Read this passage, and then answer the question that follows it:
[Enter RODERIGO.]
Iago: How now, Roderigo!
Roderigo: I do not find that thou deal’st justly with me.
Iago: What in the contrary?
Roderigo: Every day thou daff’st me with some device, lago; and rather, 5
as it seems to me now, keep’st from me all conveniency than
suppliest me with the least advantage of hope. I will indeed,
no longer endure it; nor am I yet persuaded to put up in peace
what already I have foolishly suffer’d.
Iago: Will you hear me, Roderigo? 10
Roderigo: Faith, I have heard too much; for your words and performances
are no kin together.
Iago: You charge me most unjustly.
Roderigo: With nought but truth. I have wasted myself out of my means.
The jewels you have had from me to deliver to Desdemona 15
would half have corrupted a votarist. You have told me she
hath receiv’d them, and return’d me expectations and comforts
of sudden respect and acquaintance; but I find none.
Iago: Well; go to; very well.
Roderigo: Very well! go to! I cannot go to, man, nor ’tis not very well; by 20
this hand, I say ’tis very scurvy, and begin to find myself fopt in
it.
Iago: Very well.
Roderigo: I tell you ’tis not very well. I will make myself known to
Desdemona. If she will return me my jewels, I will give over my 25
suit and repent my unlawful solicitation; if not, assure yourself I
will seek satisfaction of you.
Iago: You have said now.
Roderigo: Ay, and said nothing but what I protest intendment of doing.
Iago: Why, now I see there’s mettle in thee; and even from this 30
instant do build on thee a better opinion than ever before. Give
me thy hand, Roderigo. Thou hast taken against me a most
just exception; but yet, I protest, I have dealt most directly in
thy affair.
Roderigo: It hath not appear’d. 35
Iago: I grant, indeed, it hath not appear’d; and your suspicion is not
without wit and judgment. But, Roderigo, if thou hast that in
thee indeed, which I have greater reason to believe now than
ever – I mean purpose, courage, and valour – this night show
it; if thou the next night following enjoy not Desdemona, take 40
me from this world with treachery, and devise engines for my
life.
Roderigo: Well, what is it? Is it within reason and compass?
Iago: Sir, there is especial commission come from Venice to depute
Cassio in Othello’s place. 45
Roderigo: Is that true? Why, then Othello and Desdemona return again to
Venice.
Iago: O, no; he goes into Mauritania, and taketh away with him the
fair Desdemona, unless his abode be linger’d here by some
accident; wherein none can be so determinate as the removing 50
of Cassio.
Roderigo: How do you mean removing of him?
Iago: Why, by making him uncapable of Othello’s place – knocking
out his brains.
Roderigo: And that you would have me to do? 55
Iago: Ay, an if you dare do yourself a profit and right.
(from Act 4, Scene 2)
How does Shakespeare strikingly portray Roderigo and Iago at this moment in the play?
Or 5(b) Explore how Shakespeare vividly conveys the strength of Desdemona’s love for Othello.
